text.p: These are the leading stories in the Kenyan press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Kenya's government defends its position over invoking the Public Security Act, saying it was necessary to enable people to respond quickly and inexpensively to famine.
- Opposition leader Michael Kijana Wamalwa, denies having ever cleared business tycoon Ketan Somaia to make a multi -million dollar South African deal.
- The Law Society of Kenya and local Chapter of Jurists demand an immediate revocation of emergency provisions, arguing the government is likely to abuse them in an election year.
- More than 7,000 residents of Soweto slum area in Nairobi go to court seeking orders to restrain a business tycoon from evicting them.
- Attorney General Amos Wako has until Friday this week to give the High Court details of negotiations on the national status of Islamic political activist Sheikh Khalid Balala.
- Charity Ngilu, an opposition member of parliament, finally declares that she is ready to stand for presidency.
- A cross section of Kenyans react to opposition Social Democratic Party's announcement that it intends to resort to violence.
- A 55-year old man alleged to have offered his 14-year old niece as a human sacrifice to bring him business prosperity appears before a Mombasa court.
- The United States government pledges its support the Kenyan Government's declaration of a national famine disaster. ($1=55 Kenyan shillings)
